body.p: This is a full and timely response to the Office Action of July 31, 2024. Reexamination and reconsideration in view of the foregoing amendments and following remarks is respectfully solicited.

With the above amendments, claims 1-7 and 9-20 are now pending, with claims 1 and 13 being independent claims. In the above amendments, claims 1, 9, 10 and 12 have been amended, and claim 8 has been cancelled.
Claims 1-20 were rejected on the ground of nonstatutory obviousness-type double

patenting as being unpatentable over claims 1-17 of U.S. Patent No. 11,511,879. However, the Office Action noted that a timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321 may be used to overcome an actual or provisional rejection based on nonstatutory double patenting provided the reference application or patent either is shown to be commonly owned with the examined application, or claims an invention made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of a joint research agreement. Accordingly, applicants have submitted a web based eTerminal Disclaimer to the cited U.S. Patent No. 11,511,879. Applicants thus submit that the double patenting rejections have been overcome.
In the Office Action, claims 1-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as allegedly

being directed to an abstract idea without significantly more. The Office Action noted that the determination of whether a claim recites patent ineligible subject matter generally follows a two-step inquiry. In general, STEP 1 is to determine if a claim falls within one of four statutory categories (see MPEP 2106.03). Then, STEP 2 is to determine if the claim recites a judicial exception without reciting additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception (see MPEP 2106.04).
As described in the Office Action, STEP 2 is further divided into STEP 2A (PRONG I), STEP 2A (PRONG II), and STEP 2B. Specifically, STEP 2A (PRONG I) is to determine if a

claim recites a judicial exception, e.g., an abstract idea, law of nature or natural phenomenon (see MPEP 2106.04(II)(A) 1). If the claim recites a judicial exception, then STEP 2A (PRONG II) is to determine if the claim recites additional elements that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application (see MPEP 2106.04(II)(A)(2). Finally, Step 2B is to determine if the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. (see MPEP 2106.05).

In rejecting claims 1-20 under 35 U.S.C.. § 101 the Office Action admitted that claims 1-20 are directed to a statutory category. However, the Office Action then alleged that when analyzed under STEP 2A (PRONG I) claim 1 recites abstract mental processes, including:
provide an energy state model of the aircraft;
determine, a first measured value ...
execute at least one flight maneuver .... ,
generate a predicted energy change ... ;
determine a second measured value .... ;
generate an adjustment

Specifically, the Office Action alleged that the foregoing bolded limitations constitute a "mental process" because under its broadest reasonable interpretation, the claim covers performance of the limitation in the human mind. Specifically, the Office Action alleged that "provide", "determine", "execute", and "generate" in the context of this claim encompasses an operator looking at data and generating a simple judgment, and the Office thus concluded that the claim recites at least one abstract idea.
The Office Action then alleged that when analyzed under STEP 2A (PRONG II) that

claim 1 is not integrated into a practical application. Specifically, the Office Action alleged that while the claims include additional limitations beyond the alleged abstract idea ("system", "storage", "processors") do not integrate the limitations into a practical application.

Finally, the Office Action then alleged that when analyzed under STEP 2B that claim 1 does not include additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. Specifically, the Office Action alleged that the additional limitations ("system", "storage", "processors") represent mere generic computer components, and that applying mental processes to a generic computer component cannot provide an inventive component. i
Applicants respectfully disagree and submit that the amended claims are patent

eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Specifically, applicants submit that the amended claims recite patent eligible subject matter, pursuant to the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance" (hereinafter, the 2019 Guidelines).

First, applicants note that independent claim 1 has been amended above to more clearly tie the claims to the operation of an aircraft. Specifically, claim 1 has been amended to recite a "sensor system configured for measuring a flight characteristic of the aircraft" and that the one or more processors are configured to execute instructions to "determine a first measured value of a flight characteristic of the aircraft at a first position of the aircraft using the sensor system" and to "determine a second measured value of the flight characteristic of the aircraft at the second position using the sensor system". Claim 1 further recites that the one or more processors are configured to execute instructions to "generate an adjustment to the energy state model based on the first measured value, the second measured value, and the determined specific excess power error (PSerror)". Similar limitations are found in independent claim 13.

Applicants submit that in the present case these amended claims recite additional elements that both "integrate the judicial exception into a practical application" under STEP 2A (PRONG II) and "amount to significantly more" than the judicial exception under STEP 2B. As such, the amended claims clearly meet the requirements for eligibility of claims under § 101 when properly evaluated under the revised 2019 guidelines.
With regard to Step 2A, applicants submit that the "mental steps" alleged as being

abstract ideas are integrated into the specific application of adjusting an energy state model of the aircraft. As described in applicant's specification, the energy state model can be used by the avionics system of an aircraft to predict energy states of the aircraft, and adjusting the model as recited facilitates the accounting of real world variances in performance. See applicant's
specification at paragraph 0029.

Furthermore, applicants submit that the pending claims do not seek to "tie up" mathematical concepts as whole, but instead limit the use of the concepts to the specific application of adjusting energy state models based on specific measured values from the sensor system and the specific excess power error (PSerror).
Thus, these and other limitations found in the independent claims clearly and

unambiguously indicate that each independent claim as a whole integrates the alleged judicial exception into a practical real-world application of adjusting an energy state model based on specific measured values from the sensor system and the specific excess power error (PSerror). As such, applicants submit that the claims meet the analysis under STEP 2A, and thus satisfy the subject matter eligibility requirement of § 101.

Furthermore, even if the claimed limitations were not sufficiently integrated into the practical application of checking accuracy on an air data probe system and appropriately responding to detected problems the claims would still be patentable under STEP 2B guidelines as they recite additional elements that amount to "significantly more" than the judicial exception. Specifically, the various claims recite the calculation of a predicated excess power (PSpredicted) and specific excess power error (PSerror) and the use of the those values . Furthermore, the various claims recite specific techniques for adjusting the energy state model, including changing the value describing the gross weight of the aircraft, using specific airspeeds, and predicted values. Applicants submit that techniques that are recited in the pending claims go significantly beyond the well-understood, routine, and conventional activities in the field, and as such meet the requirements under STEP 2B.

Furthermore, as the Supreme Court has noted, "it is consistent with the general rule that patent claims 'must be considered as a whole."' Alice Corp., 134 S. Ct. at 2355, 110 USPQ2d at 1981 (quoting Diamond v. Diehr, 450 U.S. 175, 188, 209 USPQ 1, 8-9 (1981)). Thus, to determine if a claim recites "significantly more" than the judicial exceptions all of the elements of the claim must be considered in combination. Thus, even if one element does not amount to "significantly more" on its own, it can still amount to "significantly more" when considered in combination with the other elements of the claim. See, e.g., Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect,

827 F.3d 1042, 1051, 119 USPQ2d 1370, 1375 (Fed. Cir. 2016) (process reciting combination of individually well-known freezing and thawing steps was "far from routine and conventional" and thus eligible); BASCOM Global Internet Servs. v. AT&T Mobility LLC, 827 F.3d 1341, 1350, 119 USPQ2d 1236, 1242 (Fed. Cir. 2016) (inventive concept may be found in the non- conventional and non-generic arrangement of components that are individually well-known and conventional).

Thus, claims that include specific limitations beyond what is well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or include unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application will have "significantly more" than the judicial exception. See BASCOM Global Internet v. AT&T Mobility LLC, 827 F.3d 1341, 1350-51, 119 USPQ2d 1236, 1243 (Fed. Cir. 2016) and MPEP 2106.05(d).

In summary, the pending claims are directed toward aircraft and avionics systems on aircraft, and abstract ideas are integrated into the specific application of adjusting an energy state model of the aircraft. As described in applicant's specification, the energy state model can be used by the avionics system of an aircraft to predict energy states of the aircraft, and adjusting the model as recited facilitates the accounting of real world variances in performance. Applicants submit that these claimed techniques thus include specific limitations that go beyond what is well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or include unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application and thus have "significantly more" than the judicial exception
For all these reasons applicants submit that the pending claims satisfying the subject matter eligibility requirement of § 101.

In the Office Action, claims 1-7 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over H. Chamas (US Patent Publication No. 20020055816, hereinafter H. Chamas) in view of Coulmeau (US Patent Publication No. 20100274418, hereinafter Coulmeau).
In making these rejections the Office Action admitted that H. Chamas was silent about

generating a predicted energy change of the aircraft between the first position and the second position based on the at least one flight maneuver and the energy state model. However, the Office Action cited paragraphs 0074 and 0103+ as teaching this feature, and stated that it would be obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filling date of the claimed invention to modify H. Chamas by including to generate a predicted energy change of the aircraft between the first position and the second position based on the at least one flight maneuver and the energy state as taught by Coulmeau for safety performance of the aircraft. Based on this rationale, the Office Action rejected claims 1-7 under 35 U.S.C. §103.

However, the Office Action stated that claims 8-12 were allowable. Specifically, the Office Action stated that none of the cited references discloses or fairly suggests a system to determine "a specific excess power error (PSerror) of the aircraft at the second position based on the second measured value of the flight characteristic of the aircraft at the second position and the predicted specific excess power (PSpredicted) of the aircraft at the second position ..."
In response, applicants have amended independent claim 1 to recite, in part one or more data processors configured to execute the instructions to:
generate a predicted specific excess power (PSpredicted) of the aircraft between
the first position and the second position based on the at least one flight
maneuver and the energy state model;
and

p.u: determine a specific excess power error (PSerror) of the aircraft

body.p: and
generate an adjustment to the energy state model based on the first measured value, the second measured value, and the determined specific excess power

Applicants note that these added limitations to amended independent claim 1 are similar to those found in original claim 8, and thus amended independent claim 1 is submitted to be patentably distinct over the cited references for similar reasons to those given by the Office
Action with respect to original claim 8.

Applicants thus submit that none of the cited references, either alone or in combination, teach such a combination of features as recited in the amended independent claim 1, and that independent claims 1 and 13 are patentably distinct over the previously cited references. Furthermore, as claims 2-7 and 14-20 each depend from and include all the limitations of their respective independent claim, they are also submitted to be patentably distinct over the cited references.
Although the present communication may include alterations to the application or

claims, or characterizations of claim scope or referenced art, Applicant is not conceding in this application that previously pending claims are not patentable over the cited references. Rather, any alterations or characterizations are being made to facilitate expeditious prosecution of this application. Applicant reserves the right to pursue at a later date any previously pending or other broader or narrower claims that capture any subject matter supported by the present disclosure, including subject matter found to be specifically disclaimed herein or by any prior prosecution. Accordingly, reviewers of this or any parent, child or related prosecution history shall not reasonably infer that Applicant has made any disclaimers or disavowals of any subject matter supported by the present application.
In conclusion, for the reasons given above, all claims now presently in the application

are believed allowable and such allowance is respectfully requested. Should the Examiner have any questions or wish to further discuss this application, Applicant requests that the Examiner contact the undersigned attorney at (480) 385-5060.
